sections.html:
Jefferson County covers 530 square miles of mostly open country, with fewer than 30 residents per square mile in 2020. Louisville is the seat and largest city, and Avera, Stapleton, Wadley and Wrens are the other towns. Households average 2.58 people.

Prices are low and the headcount is shrinking. The midpoint value of an owner-occupied home is $105,400 for 2020-2024, and the mid-2025 estimate of 15,011 residents sits 4.5% under the 2020 base. The county peaked at 22,602 residents in 1920 and has lost people at every count since 1980, falling from 18,403 then to 15,709 in 2020.

With 24 permits in 2025 and 7,148 housing units at the 2020 count, 13.7% of them vacant, you are mostly competing with other older houses. Price off recent local sales rather than figures from ten years back. Where buyers are few, clean tax records and tidy paperwork help a listing move.

sections.h2: Who handles what in Jefferson County
sections.html:
Payments and bill questions go to the Tax Commissioner, 736 Peachtree Street, Louisville, GA 30434, telephone (478) 625-7736. The counter is open 8:30 to 5:00 on weekdays. For the worth of a parcel, call the Tax Assessor at (478) 625-8209.

  • Tax Commissioner: sends bills for land, business equipment, vehicles, mobile homes and timber
  • Board of Tax Assessors: receives returns, homestead forms and appeals
  • Clerk of Superior Court: its record center supplies warranty deed copies and runs the FANS alerts, at (478) 625-7922

The county commissioners and the school board set millage. The Tax Commissioner has no vote on it.

Land, buildings and business personal property are generally due November 15. If the bill is still open 90 days later, a 10% penalty is added. A homesteaded bill under $500 escapes that penalty.

Past that point the office can levy on the parcel. Staff treat that as a last resort and would rather collect another way, so if you are behind, calling early gives you the most options.

  • Mobile and modular homes have their own due date, so call the Tax Commissioner and ask which one applies to yours
  • A mobile home's tax for the year must be paid in full before a location permit is issued
  • Vehicle tax follows the owner's birthday

Owners with an approved homestead exemption may also see a one-time state homestead relief grant as a line on the bill. Rentals and homes without an exemption were left out of it.

If you hold taxable property on January 1, file at least one return between January 1 and April 1. After that, real property returns roll over at last year's value until you buy more land or build.

Business personal property works differently. Form PT-50P is filed every year, and items you have sold must be reported or the tax keeps coming. If you file a return stating a lower value and the assessors decline it, that is where your appeal begins.

  • First-time owners should bring a copy of the warranty deed to the Tax Assessor's Office
  • The office takes homestead forms any time of year, but one that arrives after April 1 starts a year later
  • An approved exemption stays in place until you move, sell or ask for another kind
  • A denial comes in writing, with the right to appeal

Where a local exemption is larger than the state's, the local one controls. The assessor's office can quote the amounts now in force.

sections.h2: How to appeal a Jefferson County value
sections.html:
When a notice of changed value arrives, mail the Board of Tax Assessors a written appeal. Call the Tax Assessor to confirm the deadline printed on your notice, and file early rather than late.

Three arguments are open to you: the property should not be taxed, the value is wrong, or it is out of line with comparable parcels. A complaint about how much tax was levied is turned away. The assessors review your letter and answer. If you still disagree, the County Board of Equalization holds a hearing, and Superior Court comes after that. Arbitration can stand in for the board, and the assessors' office will explain how to pick it.

Active farmland may be assessed at 30% of market value instead of the standard 40%. Conservation use is a second route, and it values farm, timber, sensitive or transitional land by its present use.

  • Covenant: the owner promises the Board of Tax Assessors to keep the land in that use for at least 10 years, and applications are due in April
  • Standing timber: untaxed until sold or cut, then taxed at full market value times the millage rate
  • Historic buildings: a register-listed structure and up to two surrounding acres can get preferential treatment

If you own acreage, talk to the assessor before listing so you know what the covenant asks of a new owner.

Ask the Tax Commissioner for a written payoff figure and have it paid at the closing table. A bill more than 90 days old already carries the 10% penalty, so a stale number will be too low.

The Clerk of Superior Court runs FANS, a free service you opt into that alerts you when records are filed against your property. Sign up before you list so a lien cannot show up in the middle of a contract.

For an inherited or former rental house, ask for each earlier year's balance separately so nothing older is missed. A cash buyer still wants the payoff settled and a clean recorded deed, though the sale skips lender appraisal and repair requests.

sections.h2: What to bring and what to expect
sections.html:
Most Jefferson County tax errands are quick if you arrive prepared. Bring the parcel number or the name on the deed, your mailing address, and a copy of the warranty deed if you just bought the property. For a deed copy, the Clerk's record center is the place to ask.

When you sell, expect this order: payoff request, payoff paid at closing, deed recorded, then a new owner's return to the assessors. Tell the Tax Assessor's office about the sale so bills follow the right owner.

Sellers of timber land should also know that standing timber is untaxed until it is cut or sold. Ask the Tax Commissioner whether a pending sale or harvest changes what is owed this year. The same goes for a mobile home sitting on the lot: settle its permit and its year's bill before the buyer's lender asks for proof.

faqs.q: When are Jefferson County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Generally November 15 for land, buildings and business property. After 90 days a 10% penalty applies.

faqs.q: What phone number reaches the Jefferson County Tax Commissioner?
faqs.a: (478) 625-7736. The office is at 736 Peachtree Street in Louisville, with counter hours from 8:30 to 5:00 on weekdays.

faqs.q: Is there a penalty on a small homesteaded Jefferson County bill?
faqs.a: No. The 90-day penalty skips homesteaded property whose bill is under $500.

faqs.q: When can a Jefferson County owner apply for homestead?
faqs.a: The deadline for the year is April 1. The office takes applications through the year, though a later one starts a year after.

faqs.q: Which office answers questions about value in Jefferson County?
faqs.a: Call the Tax Assessor at (478) 625-8209. The Tax Commissioner only bills and collects.
